dimming.explanationTitle: Why does the star get dimmer?
dimming.explanation1: When a planet passes between its star and us, it covers a small part of the star. That part's light never reaches us, so the star looks a little dimmer. Astronomers call this a transit.
dimming.explanation2: The bigger the planet compared with its star, the more light it blocks. Jupiter would block about 1 % of the Sun's light; Earth only about 0.008 %, less than 1 part in 10 000.
dimming.explanation3: A small star makes the same planet easier to find: Earth in front of a red dwarf five times smaller than the Sun blocks 25 times more of the star's light.
dimming.explanation4: Real stars are so far away that telescopes see them as points. We never see the planet itself: we find it because its star dims, again and again, every time the planet goes around.
dimming.keyboardHelpMove: Move the planet along its orbit

liningUp.chartTitle: The dip in the star's light
liningUp.ghostLegend: dashed: the same planet seen exactly edge-on
liningUp.randomSkyTitle: 100 stars like this one, tilted at random
liningUp.impactPattern: Passes {{value}} star radii from the centre
liningUp.tiltLimitPattern: Transits only if the orbit is within {{value}}° of edge-on.
liningUp.probabilityPattern: Chance that a random orbit lines up: {{value}} %
liningUp.explanationTitle: Why don't we see every planet transit?
liningUp.explanation1: A planet blocks its star's light only if it passes between the star and us. That needs its orbit to be seen almost exactly edge-on.
liningUp.explanation2: Tilt the orbit a little and the planet crosses the star off-centre: the transit gets shorter. Tilt it more and the planet only grazes the edge, then misses the star altogether.
liningUp.explanation3: Orbits point every which way, so only a fraction of planets transit for us: about the star's radius divided by the planet's distance. Planets close to their stars are far more likely to transit. For Earth seen from far away it is only 1 chance in 200.
liningUp.explanation4: That is why missions like Kepler and TESS watch hundreds of thousands of stars at once: to catch the few whose planets line up.

lightCurve.zoomChartTitle: One transit, zoomed in (all observed transits folded together)
lightCurve.limbDarkeningNote: The star's darker edge makes the middle of the dip deeper, so this radius comes out a little too big. Astronomers fit a model of the darkening.
lightCurve.lost: The dip is lost in the noise.
lightCurve.hint: A hint of a dip: observe more transits.
lightCurve.pointsReadoutPattern: {{points}} measurements inside the dip (one every {{cadence}} min)
lightCurve.equation: R<sub>planet</sub> = R<sub>star</sub> √depth    distance<sup>3</sup> = G M<sub>star</sub> P<sup>2</sup> ÷ 4π<sup>2</sup>    S/N = depth ÷ (σ ÷ √n)
lightCurve.explanation1: Depth: the fraction of light blocked is the planet's area divided by the star's, so the planet's radius is the star's radius times √depth. We know the star's size from its spectrum.
lightCurve.explanation2: Period: the time between dips is one orbit. With the star's mass, Kepler's third law turns it into the planet's distance from its star.
lightCurve.explanation3: Duration: how long the planet takes to cross the star. Far-out planets move slowly, so their transits last longer, but they come much less often.
lightCurve.explanation4: Noise: every measurement scatters a little. Folding many transits on top of each other and averaging shrinks the scatter by √n, so even an Earth-sized dip can stand out, given enough transits.
